Newborn pups of Meriones crassus are remarkably altricial, weighing approximately 3.35 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.35 grams] at birth. This low neonatal mass represents roughly two percent of the adult female body weight, a proportion consistent with the pattern observed in other small, desert-adapted gerbilline rodents. The modest size at parturition likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the arid environments this species inhabits, where females must balance gestation against the demands of thermoregulation and foraging in resource-poor landscapes. Post-natal development proceeds rapidly, however, with the altricial neonates gaining mass quickly on the mother's rich milk supply. The female typically nurtures a litter of four pups, a litter size that has been documented in field and captive studies alike. At a controlled body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], which corresponds to the species' normothermic resting state, the maximum reproductive rate of the Sundevall jird is realized through litters of four pups [N_R_i = litters of four pups]. This fecundity per event is matched to the frequency with which females can successfully rear young in a seasonally unpredictable environment.

The timing of reproductive events in Meriones crassus is tightly linked to the physiological conditions maintained at the species' preferred thermoneutral zone. When ambient conditions allow the animals to sustain a core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the gestation period is completed in 22 days [tg = 22 days]. This relatively short uterine development phase is typical for a rodent of this size and places the Sundevall jird among the more rapidly gestating members of the Muridae family. The compact gestation period allows females to compress the interval between successive litters, thereby maximizing annual output when resources are abundant. Field observations indicate that this timing is coupled to the onset of seasonal rains, which trigger a flush of vegetation and seed production essential for supporting the elevated energetic demands of pregnancy and subsequent lactation. The precise duration of 22 days may shift slightly with nutritional status, but the fundamental tempo of foetal development appears to be a canalized trait, robustly maintained across the species' range from the Negev Desert to the Arabian Peninsula.

Following the brief gestation period, the neonatal pups remain entirely dependent on maternal care. The transition to nutritional independence occurs after a period of suckling that, under standard conditions at a steady temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], lasts precisely 20 days after birth [tx = 20 days after birth]. At this weaning age, the pups begin to consume solid food, typically seeds and green plant material, though they may continue to nurse sporadically for a few additional days. The age at weaning in this species is notably early for a desert rodent, a trait that likely reduces the metabolic burden on the lactating female and allows her to initiate a subsequent pregnancy sooner. The parent-offspring conflict over milk provisioning appears to be resolved in favor of the mother's future reproductive opportunities, a strategy that makes ecological sense in a habitat where successful breeding windows are narrow and unpredictable. The weaned juveniles then enter a subadult phase characterized by rapid somatic growth and the gradual development of the physiological systems required for independent existence.

The progression from the weaned juvenile state to full sexual maturity spans a considerable developmental interval in the Sundevall jird. The time since birth at puberty, measured under stable thermal conditions at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], is 61 days after birth [tp = 61 days after birth]. This means that individuals born early in the breeding season can potentially reach reproductive maturity within the same calendar year, although in practice, most females delay their first mating until the following spring. The onset of gonadal activity at this age coincides with the attainment of approximately 75 percent of the adult body mass, suggesting a size threshold for reproductive competence. Captive colonies consistently report that young females begin to exhibit oestrous cycles and demonstrate lordosis behavior right around the 61-day mark, confirming that physiological readiness precedes the social and ecological opportunities for actual breeding. The relatively late puberty for a small desert rodent may be an adaptation to maximize the probability that a female is physiologically robust enough to survive the demands of gestation and lactation during her first reproductive attempt.

Adult females of Meriones crassus eventually attain a maximum recorded body mass of 158 grams [Wwi = 158 grams], though individual values range from 55 to 158 grams depending on age, nutritional history, and reproductive status. This ultimate wet weight for females places the species at the larger end of the size spectrum within the subgenus Pallasiomys. The basal metabolic rate corresponding to this body mass has been quantified through respirometry trials conducted at the species' standard thermoneutral temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Under those conditions, the maximum resting oxygen consumption is 154.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 154.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that is consistent with allometric predictions for a rodent of this size but slightly elevated relative to other gerbils, possibly reflecting the species' relatively high activity levels and digestive throughput at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. The maximum lifespan observed in captive individuals, again recorded at a stable body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], is 5.6 years [am = 5.6 years], a duration that reflects the reduced extrinsic mortality typical of protected captive environments, whereas free-ranging individuals rarely exceed three years due to high predation pressure and resource limitation. The Sundevall jird's annual reproductive output of approximately four pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately four pups per litter] combined with two litters per year [F_R_i = two litters per year] is modest compared to some murine rodents but well-matched to the carrying capacity of the species' arid habitats, where resource pulses are brief and unpredictable.
